extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in political biography, legal history, rhetoric, and public life
extracted.subtask_description: A critical-essay style set of evaluative criteria for judges, administrators, law-reformers, orators, and public writers, illustrated by the career of Lord Brougham. The page articulates what qualities make each role effective and identifies common failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges for the parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who always decide the particular case before them rightly; who have a nice insight into all that concerns it, are acute discerners of fact, accurate weighers of testimony, just discriminators of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind of judge is best for litigants: if a wise man had a good cause he would prefer it to be tried before such a judge. The criterion emphasizes factual acuity, precise case-focused judgment, and justice to the immediate parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges for the lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges who, in addition to deciding the case, give an ample exposition of principles applicable to other disputes; their judgments act as essays that go into the antecedents of controversy and supply principle for future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued by law students and the profession because such decisions provide doctrine and authority for future disputes. Anti-pattern: a judge who decides only what is strictly necessary will leave posterity without guiding principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piercing judicial precision / judicial intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge should possess piercing precision and an unerring regard for the specific case; to attain the highest judicial rank one must have years of patient reflection and a mind stored with doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay treats absence of this quality (as in Brougham) as disqualifying for 'the first rank' of judges. Scoring note: distinction between competent learning and an absorbed, doctrinal, brooding judicial intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative prudence and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: For political/administrative duties a person needs prudence and moderation in addition to energy and zeal; appetite for action alone does not equal administrative fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: Brougham's 'wildness and eccentricity' and 'want of prudence and moderation' impaired him as an administrator. Administrators must show steadiness and measured conduct, especially in secret or delicate duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political management / ability to manage men
rubrics_metrics.description: In critical political moments a brilliant manager of men is required: cool, tactful leadership that can influence sovereigns and coordinate ceremonial and practical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the anecdote of the chancellor managing the king to consent to a dissolution; guidance stresses careful handling of protocol, persuasive presentation, and readiness to bear responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-reformer: codifying skill and patient elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: A law reformer must be able to 'draw out what is necessary on paper,' bear the whole topic in mind, discriminate individual rights, and elaborate enacting and repealing clauses that will work amid complex past machinery; essentially the mind of a codifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: the 'rushing man' or agitator lacks the patient, precise, and technical habit required to produce complete, workable statutory reform. Example: Brougham exposed many abuses but produced few completed, elaborated reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-reformer: attention to minutiae and technical nicety
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful reform requires ability to distinguish with metaphysical nicety the advantage to preserve and the abuse to destroy; careful attention to detailed conveyancing and drafting is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: a reformer's proposals must be drafted so they operate correctly in complicated futures; failure to attend to conveyancing and drafting details leaves reforms imperfect or impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: imaginative stillness and brooding temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory is an imaginative art that typically requires a mind of stillness and brooding; imagination 'only works in a mind of stillness' and produces skilful narration and expressive emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: a restless, constantly active temperament (ascribed to Brougham) jars the imagination and prevents the delicate, lightly-touched pictures and sustained imaginative composition that mark great oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: fit tone for modern/parliamentary audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary oratory should favor calm didactic exposition and a conversational touch over Demosthenic vehemence; modern audiences expect suggestion and lightness rather than intense harangue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: adapt tone to audience — the ancient rhetorical tone is often out of place in modern parliamentary or popular contexts. Anti-pattern: enforcing vehemence as a universal rule leads to over-enthusiastic and unpersuasive speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: avoid over-vehemence and mechanical 'scream'
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehemence should be controlled and genuine; over-vehemence that seems like a 'scream' or machine-like haranguing lacks real feeling and diminishes persuasive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal warning: theatrical displays (kneeling, furious appeals) may provoke laughter or contempt; published performance without real feeling reads as mechanical and is ineffective for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published speeches must survive the loss of delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches intended for publication must be readable and effective without the speaker's voice, gestures, and presence; they should avoid dullness, excessive detail, and heavy sarcasm that only worked in delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: speeches crowded with transient detail and agitator-style facts may have had wartime influence but read as dull and uninformative later; authors should edit or adapt oral rhetoric before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical writing requires brooding, consecutive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract philosophy demands a brooding disposition and a still, investigating intellect capable of consecutive reasoning on delicate topics; haste leads to inconsistency and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: a writer who 'runs' (habitually rapid composition and activity) may produce many works but not works of the first class in philosophy; careful, slow thought is required for durable philosophical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: breadth of information versus extreme correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broadly active, restless mind will acquire immense general information (the outsides of many subjects) but cannot be expected to reach extreme correctness in all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment guidance: breadth is valuable and impressive, but reviewers should not expect the accuracy of a specialist; the essay frames this as a compliment tempered by caution about minor errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific interest as a cultural virtue (generational quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interest in physical science and new material discoveries is characteristic of certain generations and can reflect an active, impressible mind receptive to contemporary advancements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual note: the essay treats scientific curiosity as commendable in Brougham's generation; this is descriptive rather than prescriptive, but signals that engagement with contemporary science was a mark of intellectual vitality.
